1 What this workflow does

Spatial assays measure many cells while retaining each cell’s position in a tissue. CellCharterR groups cells into spatial domains: regions whose cells have similar molecular measurements and similar neighborhoods.

This vignette uses a portable 1,000-cell teaching subset. It is an exact seeded random subset of the canonical mouse-spleen SCE, but it is deliberately too small to reproduce or interpret the full biological result. Its purpose is to show the complete interface safely, offline, and on a CPU.

The workflow has five ideas:

  1. keep measurements, coordinates, annotations, and results together in one SingleCellExperiment (SCE);
  2. connect nearby cells separately within each physical tissue section;
  3. summarize each cell and its graph neighborhoods;
  4. repeat Gaussian-mixture clustering for candidate K values and choose a stable number of domains; and
  5. describe which cell types and domain-domain contacts are enriched.

1.1 Short glossary

  • Cell: one measured observation and one column of the SCE.
  • Marker: a measured protein feature, stored as a row of the protein assay.
  • Representation or embedding: a compact numeric description of each cell; this example uses the fixed published trVAE representation.
  • Spatial graph: links between nearby cells on the same physical slide.
  • Graph hop: one step along that graph; two hops reach neighbors of direct neighbors while excluding cells already reached sooner.
  • Domain: a cluster defined from a cell and its spatial neighborhood.
  • Enrichment: observed abundance or contact divided by its analytical expectation, displayed here as log2 fold change where stated.
  • Biological replicate/library: one independently sampled slide. It—not an individual cell—is the permutation unit for condition comparisons.

2 Load and inspect the teaching object

library(CellCharterR)
data("codex_mouse_spleen_tiny", package = "CellCharterR")
sce <- codex_mouse_spleen_tiny
sce

Each column is a cell. The protein assay contains marker intensities, reducedDims(sce)$spatial contains x/y positions, and X_trVAE is the fixed representation used by the published CellCharter tutorial.

SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(sce)
#> [1] "protein"
SingleCellExperiment::reducedDimNames(sce)
#> [1] "X_trVAE"       "spatial"       "X_cellcharter"
head(SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)[, c("sample", "condition", "cell_type")])

3 Run the SCE-first workflow

The candidate range is declared before fitting: K=2 through K=10. CellCharter’s neighboring-K calculation also fits the two boundary models needed to score that range. The tutorial uses three repeated runs to keep package builds short; a scientific analysis should retain the package default max_runs = 10 and convergence_tol = 0.01.

All Torch computation is forced to the CPU here. AutoK checkpoints are written to a temporary directory so interrupted fits can be resumed during an ordinary analysis.

checkpoint_dir <- tempfile("CellCharterR-tiny-AutoK-")

# Some sandboxed build systems cannot expose their own process ID to the
# processx dependency used by torch. Normal installations execute this branch;
# the packaged checkpoint keeps documentation rebuilds available when that
# external runtime facility is unavailable.
torch_ready <- tryCatch({
  loadNamespace("torch")
  TRUE
}, error = function(error) FALSE)

if (!torch_ready && identical(Sys.getenv("CELLCHARTERR_REQUIRE_TORCH"), "true")) {
  stop("The required CPU Torch workflow could not start in this validation run.")
}

if (torch_ready) {
  sce <- cellcharter_sce_workflow(
    sce,
    group_col = "cell_type_reduced",
    candidate_k = c(2L, 10L),
    checkpoint_dir = checkpoint_dir,
    spatial = "spatial",
    representation = "X_trVAE",
    sample_col = "sample",
    condition_col = "condition",
    graph_name = "cellcharter_graph",
    aggregated = "X_cellcharter_tiny",
    domain_col = "tiny_domain",
    n_layers = 3L,
    condition_groups = c("BALBc", "MRL"),
    n_perms = 10L,
    seed = 1L,
    autok_args = list(
      max_runs = 3L,
      convergence_tol = 0.01,
      fit_args = list(
        batch_size = 256L,
        max_iter = 20L,
        device = "cpu",
        num_threads = 1L
      ),
      predict_args = list(batch_size = 256L, device = "cpu")
    )
  )
} else {
  message("Torch runtime unavailable in this build process; using the validated tiny checkpoint.")
  sce <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "codex_mouse_spleen_tiny_workflow.rds",
    package = "CellCharterR", mustWork = TRUE
  ))
}

The graph is stored in colPairs(), the aggregate representation in reducedDims(), domain labels in colData(), and fitted-stage provenance and statistical results in metadata().

SingleCellExperiment::colPairNames(sce)
#> [1] "cellcharter_graph"
SingleCellExperiment::reducedDimNames(sce)
#> [1] "X_trVAE"            "spatial"            "X_cellcharter"     
#> [4] "X_cellcharter_tiny"
table(SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)$tiny_domain)
#> 
#>   0   1 
#> 508 492
names(S4Vectors::metadata(sce)$CellCharterR$results)
#> [1] "enrichment"            "nhood_enrichment"      "diff_nhood_enrichment"

The graph was built independently for every slide before applying one global distance cutoff. This is essential: geometrically close coordinates from two different tissue sections are not biological neighbors. The following check must be TRUE.

pairs <- SingleCellExperiment::colPair(sce, "cellcharter_graph")
sample_id <- as.character(SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)$sample)
all(sample_id[S4Vectors::from(pairs)] == sample_id[S4Vectors::to(pairs)])
#> [1] TRUE

X_cellcharter_tiny concatenates the original representation with exclusive one-, two-, and three-hop means. “Exclusive” means that a cell reached in one hop is not counted again in the two-hop block. These features let the GMM distinguish cells with similar marker states but different tissue contexts.

4 Diagnose the choice of K

AutoK compares solutions at neighboring K values with the Fowlkes–Mallows score. Peaks suggest comparatively stable resolutions; they are diagnostics, not biological proof. The selected K is the highest mean stability, with the first K used to break ties.

autok <- S4Vectors::metadata(sce)$CellCharterR$autok$tiny_domain
cellcharter_autok_best_k(autok)
#> [1] 2
cellcharter_plot_autok_stability(autok, k_range = 2:10) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

5 Map the teaching domains

xy <- as.data.frame(SingleCellExperiment::reducedDim(sce, "spatial"))
names(xy)[1:2] <- c("x", "y")
xy$domain <- SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)$tiny_domain
xy$sample <- SummarizedExperiment::colData(sce)$sample
xy <- xy[xy$sample %in% c("BALBc-1", "MRL-4"), , drop = FALSE]

ggplot2::ggplot(xy, ggplot2::aes(x, y, colour = domain, shape = domain)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~sample) +
  ggplot2::coord_equal() +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "Domain", title = "BALBc-1 and early MRL-4 teaching slides") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

The redundant shape encoding and the count table below keep domain identity available when colours cannot be distinguished.

as.data.frame(table(sample = xy$sample, domain = xy$domain))
#>     sample domain Freq
#> 1  BALBc-1      0   93
#> 2  BALBc-2      0    0
#> 3  BALBc-3      0    0
#> 4    MRL-4      0   49

#> 6    MRL-6      0    0

#> 9    MRL-9      0    0
#> 10 BALBc-1      1   25

#> 17   MRL-8      1    0

Do not interpret this map as a mouse-spleen reproduction: random subsampling changes the spatial graph and therefore its neighborhoods.

6 Inspect enrichment results

The cell-type result compares the observed cell-type proportion inside each domain with the cohort-wide expectation. Neighborhood enrichment is directed: row-domain contact with column-domain need not have the same normalized value as the reverse direction. Differential neighborhood enrichment permutes the condition assignment at the sample/library level, never cell by cell.

results <- S4Vectors::metadata(sce)$CellCharterR$results
round(results$enrichment$value$enrichment, 2)
#>                        0     1
#> B cells            -0.65  0.46
#> B220(+) DN T cells  0.23 -0.29
#> CD11c(+) B cells    -Inf -1.56
#> CD31(hi) vascular   -Inf -1.56
#> CD4(+) T cells      0.52 -0.86
#> CD8(+) T cells      0.60 -1.09
#> DCs                 0.22 -0.27
#> erythroblasts      -0.42  0.33
#> F4/80(+) mphs      -0.30  0.26
#> FDCs                -Inf  1.02
#> granulocytes        0.21 -0.26
#> marginal zone mphs  0.71 -1.56
#> megakaryocytes     -0.02  0.02
#> NK cells            -Inf  1.02
#> other               0.33 -0.45
#> plasma cells        0.66 -1.30
#> stroma             -0.07  0.07
round(results$nhood_enrichment$value$enrichment, 2)
#>      0    1
#> 0   NA 0.51
#> 1 0.49   NA
round(results$diff_nhood_enrichment$value$effect, 2)
#>       0    1
#> 0    NA 0.14
#> 1 -0.14   NA
enrichment <- results$enrichment$value$enrichment
enrichment_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(enrichment), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(enrichment_long) <- c("cell_type", "domain", "log2_fc")
ggplot2::ggplot(enrichment_long,
                ggplot2::aes(domain, cell_type, fill = log2_fc)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "grey85") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Teaching domain", y = "Cell type", fill = "log2 FC") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

Positive cells in this heatmap are more common in a domain than expected from their overall abundance; negative cells are depleted. For example, the code below reports the strongest finite enrichment and depletion in this teaching subset. These are demonstrations, not full-data biological conclusions.

finite_index <- which(is.finite(enrichment), arr.ind = TRUE)
finite_values <- enrichment[finite_index]
extreme_index <- finite_index[c(which.max(finite_values), which.min(finite_values)), , drop = FALSE]
data.frame(
  direction = c("strongest enrichment", "strongest depletion"),
  cell_type = rownames(enrichment)[extreme_index[, "row"]],
  domain = colnames(enrichment)[extreme_index[, "col"]],
  log2_fc = enrichment[extreme_index]
)
#>              direction        cell_type domain   log2_fc
#> 1 strongest enrichment             FDCs      1  1.023270
#> 2  strongest depletion CD11c(+) B cells      1 -1.561693

An enrichment value of -Inf is not a numerical failure: it means the observed proportion is zero while the expected proportion is positive, so its log2 fold change is negative infinity. The table deliberately reports finite extremes.

condition_matrices <- results$diff_nhood_enrichment$value$enrichment
condition_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(condition_matrices), function(condition) {
  value <- as.data.frame(as.table(condition_matrices[[condition]]))
  names(value) <- c("source", "target", "enrichment")
  value$condition <- condition
  value
}))
ggplot2::ggplot(condition_long,
                ggplot2::aes(target, source, fill = enrichment)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "grey85") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~condition) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Target domain", y = "Source domain",
                fill = "Observed - expected") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

Here each condition panel shows CellCharter’s directed neighborhood statistic, observed - expected; it is not a fold change. Rows are source domains and columns are target domains.

effect <- results$diff_nhood_enrichment$value$effect
effect_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(effect))
names(effect_long) <- c("source", "target", "effect")
ggplot2::ggplot(effect_long, ggplot2::aes(target, source, fill = effect)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "grey85") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Target domain", y = "Source domain",
                fill = "BALBc - MRL") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

The differential panel is the first categorical condition level minus the second (BALBc - MRL here), calculated from the condition-specific observed - expected matrices. Its empirical, unadjusted p-values are:

round(results$diff_nhood_enrichment$value$pvalue, 2)
#>     0   1
#> 0 0.0 0.2
#> 1 0.2 0.0

The ten permutations above are only a quick teaching demonstration. The CODEX reproduction uses 100, as required by the tutorial protocol.

The parity permutation deliberately reproduces CellCharter 0.2.0: libraries are drawn with replacement and empirical p-values use the historical directional count without a plus-one correction. P-values are unadjusted across domain pairs. Interpret the effect size before its p-value, and treat results as associations rather than causal interactions. For a new study, consider the documented permutation_mode = "shuffle" alternative and a suitable multiple-testing correction. Domain stability depends on the representation, spatial graph, candidate K range, and mixture initialization; K is a diagnostic resolution, not a biological truth.

7 Identity and subsetting safeguards

colPairs() endpoints, reduced dimensions, and colData() subset together with the SCE. Dataset-level fitted results in metadata(), however, no longer describe the subset. CellCharterR records ordered-cell digests and refuses to reuse such stages until they are recomputed.

smaller <- sce[, seq_len(100)]
dim(SingleCellExperiment::colPair(smaller, "cellcharter_graph"))
#> NULL
try(cellcharter_sce_aggregate(
  smaller,
  representation = "X_trVAE",
  graph_name = "cellcharter_graph",
  output = "recomputed"
))
#> Error : CellCharterR stage `graph:cellcharter_graph` is stale after cell reordering or subsetting; recompute it.

8 Moving to a real analysis

For a real dataset, keep large representations HDF5-backed, use cellcharter_sce_aggregate(..., filepath = ...), place checkpoints under a durable results directory, use max_runs = 10, and decide the K range before looking at stability. Biological conclusions require the complete dataset and appropriate replication; they must not be inferred from this teaching subset.

The companion H5AD vignette provides checksum-safe, unevaluated download code. The two official H5AD files total 600.4 MiB; reserve additional working space for HDF5 aggregation and checkpoints. The portable full SCE is 286.0 MiB on disk and about 693.7 MiB after loading. Full AutoK repeats many GMM fits, so runtime is hardware- and K-range-dependent; use a durable checkpoint directory and resume completed fits rather than restarting. The preserved full report records the publication-scale parameters and limitations. If a stage fails, first inspect its recorded seed, cell-order digest, sample field, CPU thread count, and checkpoint contract.

9 References

The full reproducibility report cites CellCharter (Varrone et al., 2024), the CODEX mouse-spleen dataset (Goltsev et al., 2018), and the pinned CellCharter 0.2.0 source commit used for parity.
